input_text:
# Co-brand card 30+ DPD: draft diagnosis (day 4, work in progress)

**Status:** working draft for the Director. Numbers come from `kpi_report_as_published.csv`, `monthly_performance.csv` and `accounts.csv`; every figure is traceable to a query in `queries/`. Tables `accounts` and `monthly_performance` are the two CSVs loaded into DuckDB.

## Headline

The 30+ DPD rate rose from 1.79% in May 2026 to 3.24% in November 2026, a rise of 1.45 points, with a spike to 4.58% in September. The KPI pack moved to reporting definitions v2 in June (denominator restricted to active accounts); I have checked the effect and the definition change does not materially change the picture, so the published series is used as the headline throughout this note.

The book was improving before the summer: the published rate fell from 2.28% in February to 1.96% in March and 1.67% in April, the lowest level in the 18 months of history, and was still 1.79% in May. The deterioration is therefore a June-onwards event, and the question is what changed in the summer.

## Reconciliation of the published series

`queries/q2_published_recon.sql` rebuilds the pack series from `monthly_performance`. It reproduces the published v1 series through May 2026 and the v2 series from June onwards; the November denominator is 5,591 accounts, matching the pack to the account. The pack numbers are therefore trustworthy and the rise is not a reporting artefact; it is in the account-level data.

## Driver 1: the August payments-platform migration (the spike)

Autopay scheduling moved to a new vendor on 4 August; ticket PAY-4471 ("subset of scheduled autopay debits not submitted") was opened on 19 August and the fix was deployed on 27 September (ops notes). The data shows exactly this (`queries/q4_autopay_and_cure.sql`, first statement):

| Month | Autopay debits attempted | Failed | Fail % | 30+ rate, autopay accounts | 30+ rate, non-autopay accounts |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-07 | 2,948 | 0 | 0.0% | 1.28% | 3.35% |
| 2026-08 | 3,025 | 359 | 11.9% | 3.09% | 3.47% |
| 2026-09 | 3,134 | 373 | 11.9% | 4.35% | 3.64% |
| 2026-10 | 3,102 | 0 | 0.0% | 2.41% | 3.99% |
| 2026-11 | 3,114 | 0 | 0.0% | 1.77% | 4.23% |

Autopay-enrolled customers are normally the best-paying part of the book (about 1.1 to 1.3% 30+ through July). For two cycles their rate more than tripled while the non-autopay rate moved by a few tenths. 416 distinct accounts had at least one failed debit. Accounts that hit a failed debit account for 61 of the 206 accounts 30+ in August (30%) and 93 of the 260 in September (36%); by November they are 14 of 181 (8%). Impacted accounts span all tiers (117 A, 152 B, 100 C, 47 D), which is what an operational failure looks like and a credit problem does not. This is the whole of the September spike and most of the August step.

## Driver 2: the spring 2026 in-store vintage (the part that stays)

The spring in-store promotion (CMP-2026-SPRING-INSTORE, March to May, instant approval at the register with the score floor lowered 20 points) booked 542 accounts with an average origination FICO of 675 against 711 for the rest of the book. Including organic in-store traffic, 1,467 accounts were opened in March to May 2026 versus a normal run-rate of about 150 a month. In November these spring accounts are 22% of the open book (1,412 of 6,358) and run at 3.97% 30+ against 2.53% for the rest of the book. Inside the vintage, the campaign accounts run at 5.33% versus 3.16% for organic accounts opened in the same months, so the lowered floor is the specific issue, not in-store acquisition in general. This vintage, not the autopay incident, is why November (3.24%) is still well above May.

Seasoning matters for how much further this goes. `queries/q3_vintage_seasoning.sql` gives the 30+ rate by months on book for the vintages opened since June 2025: 0.38% at 2 months on book, 1.36 to 1.76% at 4 to 5 months, 2.04% at 6, 2.46% at 7, 2.21% at 8, then climbing through 3.11% at 11 months to 3.58% at 15 months on book. The curve is still rising at 15 months. The spring vintage is at 6 to 8 months on book in November, so it has not reached its seasoning peak; on this curve its rate should rise a further 1.1 to 1.5 points over the next six to nine months before it levels off, which would add roughly 0.3 points to the portfolio rate.

## Which customers

By credit tier (`queries/q1_segment_rates.sql`, first statement), 30+ rate in May / September / November 2026:

| Tier | May | Sep | Nov | Nov accounts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0.65% | 2.33% | 0.76% | 1,831 |
| B | 1.20% | 2.67% | 1.83% | 2,407 |
| C | 2.51% | 6.37% | 4.96% | 1,431 |
| D | 4.85% | 7.82% | 7.04% | 739 |

Tiers A and B spiked in September and are back near their May level; the lasting deterioration is in C and D, where the spring campaign accounts concentrate. By acquisition channel (second statement) the rise is broad and roughly even: bank_direct 1.81% to 2.54%, partner_instore 1.82% to 2.91%, partner_online 1.75% to 2.88%, affiliate 1.57% to 3.20% on a base of 344 accounts. Channel as such is not a driver; the campaign vintage inside the in-store channel is. The rise is also spread across the ten largest states, so geography is not a driver.

## The September cohort has cured

`queries/q4_autopay_and_cure.sql` (second statement) follows the 260 accounts that were 30+ in September. By November, 220 of them (85%) are no longer delinquent; for the 93 autopay-impacted accounts it is 84 of 93 (90%), with only 9 still past due and in collections. The autopay part of the September cohort has fully cured, which is the pattern of a payments failure rather than a credit event, and supports telling the partner that the spike is behind us.

## Open item

Credit line program wave 3 (April, policy memo P-2026-04-CLI) increased lines for 867 accounts (221 tier B, 646 tier C). Their 30+ rate went from 3.02% in May to 5.44% in November against 1.59% to 2.46% for the rest of the book. Three quarters of the wave is tier C, so part of that gap is tier mix; I have not yet separated the line-increase effect from tier and utilization at selection. Day 5.

## Recommendations, ordered by impact

1. **To Risk and the partner: close out PAY-4471.** Confirm the fix is holding (zero failed debits in October and November), finish the collections outreach and fee reversals for the 416 impacted accounts, and give the partner the August to October explanation with the autopay table above. Cost: fee reversals already processed; otherwise negligible.
2. **To the partner and Marketing: withdraw the lowered score floor for in-store instant approval**, or restrict it to applicants who would land in tiers A and B, before the next in-store promotion. Re-review the 542 campaign accounts at 12 months on book. Cost: fewer approvals on in-store promotions; the spring campaign added about 540 accounts, of which the marginal 20-point band is the part that would be lost.
3. **To Risk: a book-wide 10% credit line decrease across all open accounts, effective with the December cycle**, to bring exposure down while the rate normalises over the next two quarters. Cost: lower spend and interchange across the portfolio and a partner conversation about customer experience; this is the fastest way to protect the loss forecast.

Next steps for day 5: close the CLI open item, build the one-pager, and quantify expected losses for the spring vintage.

structure.one_line_restatement: The published 30+ DPD rate rose 1.45 points from May to November 2026 because of two separable events, an August autopay migration failure that produced the September spike and has since cured, and a spring 2026 in-store campaign vintage booked under a lowered score floor that explains the part of the rise that remains and will get worse with seasoning; therefore close the payments ticket, withdraw the lowered floor, and cut credit lines 10% book-wide.
structure.answer_first_note: The 'Headline' section leads with a number (1.79% to 3.24%, spike to 4.58%) and a methodological reassurance about definitions v2, not with an answer. The actual answer of the diagnosis, 'two drivers: an operational failure that is over and a credit vintage that is not', first appears only as the pair of section titles 'Driver 1' and 'Driver 2' halfway down, and the asks sit in the last section under 'Recommendations, ordered by impact'. For a Director who asks 'What are you asking me to decide?' in the first minute, the top of the note should state: (a) how much of the 1.45 points is real on a consistent definition, (b) the split of that real rise between the cured autopay event and the persisting spring vintage, (c) the one decision needed now. The reconciliation paragraph and the 'book was improving before the summer' narrative belong in support, not in the headline.
structure.central_question: Why has the co-brand card 30+ DPD rate risen since May 2026, how much of the rise will persist, and what should Risk and the partner do about it?

issue_tree.sub_question: Is the rise real, i.e. how much of the published 1.79% to 3.24% move survives a consistent definition?
sub_points: Headline: KPI pack moved to definitions v2 in June (active-only denominator); 'I have checked the effect and the definition change does not materially change the picture' (asserted, no table or query shown).
Reconciliation section: queries/q2_published_recon.sql rebuilds the pack; November denominator 5,591 matches the pack to the account; 'the rise is not a reporting artefact'.
Headline paragraph 2: published rate fell 2.28% (Feb) to 1.67% (Apr), 'the book was improving before the summer', so the deterioration is 'a June-onwards event'.

issue_tree.sub_question: How much of the rise is the August payments-platform migration, and is that part over?
sub_points: Driver 1 table: 359 and 373 failed debits in Aug and Sep (11.9%), zero in Jul, Oct, Nov; autopay-account 30+ rate 1.28% to 4.35% and back to 1.77%.
416 distinct impacted accounts; impacted accounts are 61 of 206 (30%) August and 93 of 260 (36%) September 30+ accounts, 14 of 181 (8%) in November.
Impacted accounts span all tiers (117 A, 152 B, 100 C, 47 D), read as operational not credit.
'The September cohort has cured' section: 220 of 260 (85%) no longer delinquent by November; 84 of 93 (90%) of the autopay-impacted subset.
Conclusion drawn: 'This is the whole of the September spike and most of the August step.'

issue_tree.sub_question: How much of the rise is the spring 2026 in-store vintage, and how much further will it go?
sub_points: CMP-2026-SPRING-INSTORE: 542 campaign accounts, origination FICO 675 vs 711; 1,467 accounts opened Mar-May vs ~150/month run-rate.
November: spring accounts are 22% of the open book (1,412 of 6,358) at 3.97% vs 2.53% for the rest; campaign 5.33% vs organic same-month 3.16%, so the lowered floor is the specific issue.

queries/q3_vintage_seasoning.sql: curve from 0.38% at 2 MOB to 3.58% at 15 MOB, still rising; spring vintage at 6-8 MOB 'should rise a further 1.1 to 1.5 points', adding ~0.3 points to the portfolio rate.
Claim: 'This vintage, not the autopay incident, is why November is still well above May.'

issue_tree.sub_question: Which customers carry the deterioration (tier, channel, geography)?
sub_points: Tier table May/Sep/Nov from queries/q1_segment_rates.sql: A and B spike and recover; C (2.51% to 4.96%) and D (4.85% to 7.04%) stay elevated.
Channel rise is 'broad and roughly even' (bank_direct 1.81% to 2.54%, partner_instore 1.82% to 2.91%, partner_online 1.75% to 2.88%, affiliate 1.57% to 3.20%); channel is not a driver.
Spread across the ten largest states; geography is not a driver.

issue_tree.sub_question: Did the April credit line increase (wave 3) contribute?
sub_points: Open item: 867 accounts (221 B, 646 C), 30+ 3.02% in May to 5.44% in November vs 1.59% to 2.46% for the rest of the book.
Tier mix not yet separated from the line-increase effect; deferred to day 5.
Rec 1: close out PAY-4471, finish outreach and fee reversals, give the partner the autopay explanation.
Rec 2: withdraw or restrict the lowered score floor before the next in-store promotion; re-review the 542 accounts at 12 MOB.
Rec 3: book-wide 10% credit line decrease from the December cycle 'to bring exposure down while the rate normalises'.

mece_gaps: No bridge from May to November. The tree has five candidate explanations (definition change, autopay, spring vintage, CLI wave 3, ordinary seasoning of the rest of the book) but nowhere are their contributions in points added up against the 1.45-point headline. Without the bridge the reader cannot tell whether the drivers overlap or leave a residual. The residual is visible in the note's own Driver 1 table: the non-autopay 30+ rate climbs from 3.35% (Jul) to 4.23% (Nov), almost a point, and neither driver section claims that movement.

The branches overlap and the overlap is not handled. Autopay-impacted accounts (416, all tiers) and spring-vintage accounts (1,412) and CLI wave 3 accounts (867, B and C, selected in April while the spring vintage was being booked) are each measured against 'the rest of the book' as if disjoint. An account can sit in two or three of these groups; the note never shows the cross-tab, so the driver shares are not additive.

The 'Is the rise real' branch has no evidence under it. The reconciliation only shows that one denominator (5,591) matches; a consistent-definition series (v1 rule applied to all 18 months, or v2 applied to all 18 months) is the one table that would settle this branch and it is absent.

The sub-questions use three different rate definitions, so the branches are not measured in the same unit as the headline: the headline is the published v2 rate (active-only denominator) from June; queries/q1_segment_rates.sql lines 4-7 divide by count(*) of all rows including closed and charged_off; queries/q3_vintage_seasoning.sql lines 4-7 and queries/q4_autopay_and_cure.sql lines 9-14 use active plus open_no_balance (the v1 rule). The tier table, the vintage rates and the autopay rates therefore cannot be compared with each other or with the 3.24%.

The 'what should be done' branch does not descend from the diagnosis tree. Recs 1 and 2 hang from Drivers 1 and 2; Rec 3 (book-wide 10% line decrease) hangs from nothing above it, and the only branch it could hang from (CLI wave 3 / exposure) is the one marked open and unfinished.

Missing sub-question: what the partner and Risk already believe. The note says the published series is used 'throughout', and recommends 'telling the partner the spike is behind us', but never asks which figures the partner and the Director have already seen (the v2 pack numbers) and how a restated series will land.

logic_breaks.claim: 'I have checked the effect and the definition change does not materially change the picture, so the published series is used as the headline throughout this note.'
logic_breaks.where_in_material: Headline, first paragraph; relied on by every rise figure in the note (1.45 points, 4.58% spike, 'still well above May').
logic_breaks.why_it_does_not_follow: No check is presented. The headline compares a v1 number (May, denominator all open accounts, 5,966) with v2 numbers (June onward, active-only denominator; kpi_report_as_published.csv lines 13-14 show the denominator falling from 5,966 to 5,340 in a month when accounts were still being added). The data dictionary (lines 41-43) states the two rules. Recomputing from monthly_performance.csv with the v1 rule applied to every month gives May 1.79%, September 4.03%, November 2.85%: a 1.06-point rise, not 1.45, and a 4.03% peak, not 4.58%. Roughly 0.4 points of the headline is the definition change, which is material against a 1.45-point story. The structural consequence is that the opening sentence of the note is a number the analyst cannot defend as like-for-like.

logic_breaks.claim: 'queries/q2_published_recon.sql ... reproduces the published v1 series through May 2026 and the v2 series from June onwards; the November denominator is 5,591 accounts, matching the pack to the account. The pack numbers are therefore trustworthy.'
logic_breaks.why_it_does_not_follow: The query as written cannot reproduce either series. queries/q2_published_recon.sql line 9 filters to status = 'active' for all months and line 4 counts 30+ only among those active rows; the 'v1' label on line 6 is a case expression on the month, not a different denominator. Under that query May is 102/5,266 (1.94%), not the published 107/5,966, and November is 165/5,591 (2.95%), not the published 181/5,591 (3.24%). Only the denominator matches the pack; the numerator does not. 'Trustworthy' is therefore asserted on evidence that, if the reader runs it, disagrees with the pack in every month.

logic_breaks.claim: 'The book was improving before the summer ... 1.67% in April, the lowest level in the 18 months of history ... The deterioration is therefore a June-onwards event, and the question is what changed in the summer.'
logic_breaks.where_in_material: Headline, second paragraph; this framing sets the question the whole note then answers.
logic_breaks.why_it_does_not_follow: The February-to-April fall coincides with the denominator growing from 4,597 to 5,579 (kpi_report_as_published.csv lines 10-12) as the spring vintage booked 1,467 accounts at 0-2 months on book, which the note's own seasoning curve puts at 0.38% 30+. Adding a large block of accounts that cannot yet be delinquent lowers the rate mechanically; it is not evidence the book was improving, and it is the same vintage the note later blames. The 'June-onwards event' question is therefore built on a dilution effect, and it points the reader away from March-May, where Driver 2 actually originates.

logic_breaks.claim: 'By November, 220 of them (85%) are no longer delinquent ... The autopay part of the September cohort has fully cured.'
logic_breaks.where_in_material: The September cohort has cured; also the basis for Rec 1's 'tell the partner the spike is behind us'.
logic_breaks.why_it_does_not_follow: queries/q4_autopay_and_cure.sql lines 33-36 define 'still delinquent' as November rows with status = 'active' and dpd_bucket >= 30, and define 'cured' as everything else. Everything else includes accounts that charged off, closed, or have no November row. Following the 260 September 30+ accounts in monthly_performance.csv to November: 162 are current (138 active, 24 open_no_balance), 49 are still 30+ (40 active, 9 open_no_balance), 29 are charged_off and 20 have no November row. 'No longer delinquent' is thus 62%, not 85%, and the 29 charge-offs are the opposite of a cure. The conclusion 'payments failure rather than a credit event' may still be right for the autopay subset, but the evidence as cited does not establish it.

logic_breaks.claim: 'This is the whole of the September spike and most of the August step.'
logic_breaks.why_it_does_not_follow: The note's own numbers give impacted accounts 93 of the 260 September 30+ accounts (36%). The September spike over July is 260 minus 138 = 122 accounts; even attributing all 93 impacted accounts to the incident leaves about 30 excess accounts, and the non-autopay rate in the same table rises 3.35% to 3.64% to 3.99% to 4.23% through November, which the autopay story cannot explain. 'Whole' is a stronger word than the table supports; the table supports 'most of the spike and none of the trend underneath it'.

logic_breaks.claim: 'On this curve its rate should rise a further 1.1 to 1.5 points over the next six to nine months ... which would add roughly 0.3 points to the portfolio rate.'
logic_breaks.why_it_does_not_follow: queries/q3_vintage_seasoning.sql groups by open_month and takes max(months_on_book), so each point on the 'curve' is a different vintage observed once, at its own age, all measured over the same calendar months. The 6-8 MOB points are the spring 2026 vintage itself; the 11-15 MOB points are the June-October 2025 vintages, booked under standard policy, observed during the August-September autopay incident. Projecting the spring vintage along that line assumes it follows older, better-underwritten vintages and that their elevated late readings are seasoning rather than the incident. Neither is shown. The 0.3-point forecast is the only forward-looking number in the note and it rests on a cross-section read as a trajectory.

logic_breaks.claim: Rec 3: 'a book-wide 10% credit line decrease across all open accounts ... this is the fastest way to protect the loss forecast', presented as a recommendation ordered by impact.
logic_breaks.why_it_does_not_follow: Nothing above it in the note identifies exposure or line size as a driver. Driver 1 is an operational failure described as cured; Driver 2 is a 542-account campaign segment; the tier table shows A and B back near May levels. The one place lines appear in the diagnosis is the CLI wave 3 open item, which the note explicitly says is not yet separated from tier mix. A book-wide action therefore has no parent in the issue tree, and 'ordered by impact' is contradicted by item 1 being the negligible-cost close-out of an incident that has already ended.

frameworks_used.why_here: The note has an implicit SCQA and the Situation is wrong, which misdirects the Question. S = 'book was improving to 1.67% in April', C = 'then rose to 3.24% with a 4.58% spike', Q = 'what changed in the summer'. Both S and C are built from a series whose denominator rule changes in June and whose spring months are diluted by 1,467 brand-new accounts. Fix the S and C (one consistent series, May 1.79% to November about 2.85%, spike about 4.03%) and the Question changes from 'what happened in the summer' to 'how much of a roughly one-point rise is a cured payments incident and how much is a March-May underwriting decision', which is the question the two driver sections actually answer. Getting the opening thirty seconds right here changes which number the Director remembers.

The note is organised as a tour (headline number, reconciliation, driver, driver, segments, cure, open item, recs) rather than answer-first. Running 'so what' up each branch exposes that the three recommendations do not all connect to the findings: Recs 1 and 2 are the so-what of Drivers 1 and 2, but Rec 3 has no finding beneath it and the CLI open item has no recommendation above it. Restacking as 'answer at the top, two drivers beneath, evidence beneath those' would put the ask on line one, move the reconciliation and the seasoning projection into supporting evidence, and make the missing bridge from May to November visible as the one slide the argument still needs.
